title: A walk on a graph, balanced edge by edge

prereqs.why: Detailed balance is what makes the answer a guess that can be checked in one line instead of a linear system.
Detailed balance implies stationarity, which is the theorem being used.
The chain has to be irreducible for the stationary distribution to be the unique one, and a connected graph is exactly that.

statement:
Let $G$ be the graph on vertices $\{1,2,3,4\}$ with edges

$$\{1,2\},\quad \{2,3\},\quad \{3,4\},\quad \{1,3\}.$$

A walker at vertex $v$ moves to a uniformly chosen neighbour of $v$, so

$$p_{v,w} = \frac{1}{\deg(v)} \ \text{ if } \{v,w\} \text{ is an edge}, \qquad 0 \text{ otherwise.}$$

$G$ is connected, so the chain is irreducible and has a unique stationary
distribution $\pi$.

**Detailed balance** says: if a distribution $\pi$ satisfies
$\pi_v p_{v,w} = \pi_w p_{w,v}$ for every pair, it is stationary. Guess a
$\pi$ proportional to something about each vertex, check the balance
equations, and normalise.

Give $\pi_3$ exactly.
hints: Write down the degree of each of the four vertices first. Vertex 3 is the busiest.
Try $\pi_v \propto \deg(v)$ and substitute into $\pi_v p_{v,w} = \pi_w p_{w,v}$. Both sides collapse to the same thing.
With $\pi_v = \deg(v)/c$, the balance equation reads $\tfrac{\deg(v)}{c}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\deg(v)} = \tfrac{\deg(w)}{c}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\deg(w)}$, which is $1/c = 1/c$.
The normalising constant is the sum of all the degrees, which is twice the number of edges.

payload.label: $\pi_3 =$
payload.syntax: A number or a fraction. Arithmetic is fine.
